extracted.intended_audience: researchers in analytic number theory / mathematicians working on zeros of the Riemann zeta-function
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing a research note on large gaps between consecutive nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, including unconditional bounds and conditional results based on moment conjectures; includes a withdrawn-version note explaining a flaw. Intended for readers checking correctness, sharpness of inequalities, and dependence on hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous proof of unconditional bounds (explicit constants)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this paper, we prove the lower bound of the unconditional large gap is 3.5555 which improves the obtained value 3.079 in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of unconditional quantitative bounds must be supported by complete, verifiable proofs deriving the stated numerical constants; comparisons with prior literature should be explicit. Include derivations that allow independent checking of how the numeric constant (here 3.5555) is obtained from the arguments. Avoid hiding numeric steps or relying on unstated approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly state conditional hypotheses and derive explicit conditional formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: On the hypothesis that the moments of the Hardy Z-function and its derivatives are correctly predicted we establish a new explicit formula of the gaps and use it to establish some lower bounds for k=3,4,...,15.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting conditional results, explicitly state the conjectures or moment-predictions on which the conclusions depend, give the exact form of any 'explicit formula' obtained, and enumerate the derived consequences (e.g., lower bounds for specific k values). Make the dependency on the hypothesis transparent so readers can see which parts are conditional and which are unconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inequalities with sharp (or justified) constants
rubrics_metrics.description: The main results are proved by employed an integral inequality with a best constant proved by David Boyd. (Comment: The inequality applied in this paper in not sharp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof relies on an inequality or a numerical 'best constant', the sharpness and provenance of that constant must be established or justified. Cite the precise source (e.g., Boyd) and verify applicability; if the inequality is not sharp for the application, assess how that affects final numeric bounds. Anti-pattern: using a non-sharp inequality (or misapplying a cited 'best constant') that invalidates the claimed numeric improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent status and correction of errors (withdrawal / erratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: This paper has been withdrawn by the author. The inequality applied in this paper in not sharp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a substantive flaw is discovered (e.g., misuse of an inequality that undermines main conclusions), authors should transparently correct the record via erratum or withdrawal and provide a clear explanation of the error and its effect on the results. For readers/evaluators, check the submission history, comments, and withdrawal notes to understand which claims remain valid.
